title_en: The 30 First-Person Shooter Masterpieces You Need To Play, From Old-School Pioneers to Cutting-Edge Blasters
summary_en: From the original corridor shooter pioneers to the incredibly sophisticated genre hybrids of the 2020s, these are the 30 first-person shooter masterpieces you need to play.
body_en:
Part of the promise of video games is putting yourself in another world, taking control of a character and experiencing adventure and excitement through their eyes. No genre takes this premise quite so literally as the first-person shooter, a pillar of the medium and a fundamental building block of the entire industry. There’s no shortage of shooters out there, but a select few stand above the rest as high-water marks for the art form. These are the 30 first-person shooter masterpieces you need to play
Everything has to begin somewhere. For the first-person shooter, the primordial soup was a group of high school students working at a NASA study program in 1973. They created Maze War, a series of corridors you explored in hunt of another player to shoot. Unbeknownst to those students, they had triggered the start of an evolutionary chain that would lead to the creation of 100-player Warzone lobbies where victorious teenagers teabag the dead.
But the first of something is rarely the best, nor the most influential. And so we look a little further ahead in the timeline to find the real pioneers. Wolfenstein 3D , id Software’s 1992 classic, is undoubtedly one of them. But that Nazi-plagued labyrinth was quickly overshadowed a year later by our first true masterpiece.
If the FPS has a main character, it’s the marine that sits in the middle of Doom ’s HUD. A representation of not just your unseen protagonist but also your health, his chiselled features are progressively marred by blood and bruises as you push on through some of the most focused firefights the genre has ever had to offer. Free from the burden of storytelling and lore, Doom is all about the kill.
And there are so, so many kills. The garish corridors of Mars (and, later, Hell) are perfectly formed containers for exciting, kinetic, and challenging combat encounters. Back in 1993 we couldn’t even look up, but that didn’t stop id Software from assaulting us with an array of demons, both grounded and flying. Survival against such odds is made possible thanks to a small arsenal of weapons so purposeful in their design it makes modern shooters, with their army supply inventory, look like criminal waste – who needs (or even wants) 15 different SMGs when you can have the best shotgun in the business to gun down imps, and the chaingun with an RPM perfectly calibrated to interrupt a cacodemon’s fiery belches?
The early days of first-person shooters were an abstract affair, with blank-slate protagonists gliding through spartan research facilities and gothic labyrinths. The setting was more of a suggestion to keep you moving, bleary brick textures on ray-casted walls for your mute hero to grunt against in search of secret doors. Gamers were more than happy with the arrangement until a potty-mouthed, stogie-chomping, mildly misogynistic meathead showed them a better way.
Apogee’s Duke Nukem 3D brought their EGA sidescrolling hero to a new dimension in the first hit shooter that dared to have a personality. Fully-voiced by Jon St. John, Duke oozed charisma, cracking jokes and one-liners appropriated from ‘80s action cinema. Fittingly, the first level sees Duke dropped onto an LA rooftop and fighting his way into an infested movie theater full of interactive objects, a far cry from the castles and space bases of his contemporaries. This was a first-person shooter that took place in our world, at our time, in places we could actually recognize, albeit with more burning barrels and floating powerups. The first-person POV was designed to help players embody their avatar, and Duke 3D was the first to make the world they inhabited just as immersive.
1999 is arguably the most important year in multiplayer history. Id Software continued to shape the bedrock of the entire FPS genre with Quake 3 Arena, an outstanding multiplayer hit whose engine would go on to power the behemoth that is Call of Duty. But just a few weeks earlier, Epic Games had shipped Unreal Tournament – the studio’s first dedicated PvP game, and the very first cog in the machine that would eventually become Fortnite.
But even 27 years and hundreds of innovators later, Unreal Tournament remains perfectly formed. It is a library of phenomenal level design, with the industrial ramps and slime pools of DM-Deck16 providing the perfect arrangement of height and hazard for the ultimate deathmatch, and the symmetrical halves of the incredibly lean Facing Worlds providing the blueprint for every great Capture the Flag map. The arsenal is fantastic (particularly the ricocheting pellets ejected by the Flak Canon) and the action a gore-soaked adrenaline rush, but it’s the precision-engineered maps that make Unreal Tournament an immortal classic.
Valve does things differently. That’s a truth that goes right back to the developer’s very first game. Doom, Quake, and Unreal all have some kind of story wrapper, but they’re utilitarian – the gunplay is what drives them. Half-Life proved that narrative could be more than just a framework for FPS games. Gordon Freeman’s escape from a laboratory under siege is one of the richest stories a shooter has ever told, and it does it with barely any dialogue. Instead, the very walls and floors of the Black Mesa Research Facility provide the script – each new corridor and chamber the stage for a dramatic alien incursion or eerily quiet reveal. While Half-Life technically does have levels, the lab flows as one whole, continuous space, which cements it as a genuine place rather than a series of maps. The result is an experience that feels incredibly real, which only enhances the horror of your work colleagues being transformed into zombies.
Doom has remained a titan of shooters because it never ages. It’s constantly being reinvented and updated, typically by modding fans who have created some of the original game’s greatest levels. But id Software itself has also approached its hellish masterpiece in brand new ways, and the exceptional 2016 reboot of Doom is gaming’s best example of how to revitalise a franchise.
The hyper-specific focus of the original game remains, but it’s elevated to impossible new heights by the punchiest gunplay you’ve ever pulled the trigger of. Your trusty shotgun rips demons apart, but when that’s not enough you can literally dig your hands in, tearing flesh to not just kill, but to replenish your own life force. This reboot arrived on the tail end of an era where shooters had been obsessed with cover and hunkering down to recover health. Doom said f*ck all that – to mend, you need to maul. And by tearing up the rule book, it restored the franchise’s HP to 100%.
So far, this could easily be mistaken for a list of the best PC games. When it comes to accuracy, the mouse is king, so of course many of the best shooters can be found on PC. But as soon as the analogue stick was invented, a whole new world was unlocked on consoles. While modern logic dictates that you need two sticks to make a shooter work, Nintendo has never been one for conventional thinking. The Nintendo 64 controller had just one analogue stick, and that carried us through one of the most seminal FPS games of all time…
Hailing from an era of Doom clones and developed by a team of novices at Rare, in hindsight it’s incredible that GoldenEye 007 became an iconic trailblazer. Rather than a straight up shooting gallery, its campaign acknowledged James Bond’s secret service employment through encouragement of stealth – there are no health packs here, and gunfire will summon curious guards, so tactical elimination of enemies is often the name of the game. Thankfully, an array of clever gadgets and then-novel tricks, like a sniper rifle with telescopic scope, offered methods of survival beyond just equipping the Klobb SMG for a bit of pray-and-spray.
Of course, the Klobb’s ridiculous fire rate proved incredibly useful in GoldenEye’s unforgettable multiplayer. Featuring a collection of modes with objectives inspired by Bond’s adventures, such as You Only Live Twice’s two-lives-per-player, and The Man With The Golden Gun’s instakill 24-karat blaster, this was (and still is) the splitscreen champion of the world.
Nintendo may be best known as the home of the world’s greatest platformers, but GoldenEye proved you didn’t need a PC to play a groundbreaking FPS. A generation later, the big N continued to innovate: 2002’s Metroid Prime became the GameCube’s most essential shooter by stripping back the shooting.
Yes, you are of course equipped with Samus Aran’s trademark arm cannon, and the surface of Tallon IV is home to plenty of enemies in need of blasting, but Metroid Prime takes a quieter approach to the FPS, prioritizing exploration over explosions. An effective translation of the series’ 2D values into a 3D world, puzzles and platforming are your core verbs here. Unlocking new equipment allows you to enter and survive new regions, and demolishing bosses arms you with an enjoyable selection of tools that ensures the galaxy’s coolest bounty hunter will take down her mark.
Bungie wanted to call its Xbox debut simply “Halo”. It was Microsoft that insisted on the “Combat Evolved” subtitle. As clunky and unnecessary as that addition is, though, it’s impossible to deny that it summarised the entire experience in two words. Back in 2001, Halo was an astonishing leap forward, and its advancements still have the capacity to enthrall a quarter century later. The campaign offers a perfectly balanced blend of tight corridor firefights and freeform, vehicle-friendly sandbox areas. Every single weapon not only feels punchy but fulfills a specific role, from the shield-splitting plasma rifle to the tank-busting SPNKr. Bungie’s star achievement, though, is its enemy AI, which turned the various ranks of the Covenant into a coherent fighting force, working together to flank, flush, and finish you. Responding realistically to incoming grenades and dwindling numbers, the Covenant breathes a genuine sense of life into Combat Evolved’s campaign.
Of course, the multiplayer side of Halo didn’t need artificial intelligence – it had real players. While the explosive mix of Xbox Live and Halo 2 was yet to come, the original game’s splitscreen multiplayer remains a supreme example of how to upgrade classic deathmatch with refined maps, phenomenal weapons, and the wildcard addition of a swerving Warthog.
In the wake of Halo’s arrival, the race was on for PlayStation to find its own “Halo killer”. Several developers attempted, every one of them failed. But that’s not to say the hunt didn’t produce greatness. Guerrilla Games’ Killzone 2 is a master of hard, gritty sci-fi, its WW2-in-space aesthetic elevated to great heights thanks to once-mindblowing graphical quality that remains impressive to this day. All that lends the campaign a distinct atmosphere, but the real joy here is something that spans both single and multiplayer: really, really good guns. There are obvious favourites, like the skull-shattering M4 Revolver and the infantry-chewing StA-3 LMG, but every single one of Killzone 2’s weapons is lovingly crafted, with exceptional reload animations, fantastic audio design, and unique approaches that ensure every single one of them fulfills a distinct battlefield purpose.
It wasn’t enough for Bungie to rewrite the FPS rulebook once. With Destiny , it took many of the ideas that fuelled Halo – unrivalled gunfeel, large environments, deep lore, and intense arena multiplayer – and spliced it with DNA from loot-driven games like Diablo and MMOs like World of Warcraft. The result was initially imperfect, with mission design that felt empty compared to the studio’s previous battlegrounds, as well as an over-reliance on grind. But as Destiny expanded, Bungie refined its online shooter formula, finding unique strength in raids – complex six-player co-op dungeons made up of a mix of fierce combat, cryptic puzzles, and tough boss encounters. By the time of Rise of Iron’s Wrath of the Machine and its spectacular Siege Engine, it was more than clear that Bungie had struck gold a second time.
Anyone who loves FPS games will reject the term “mindless shooter”, but there are plenty of gun games that certainly rely on reflexes more than mental aptitude. Serious Sam isn’t remotely concerned with your forward thinking or tactical planning. But, around the turn of the millenium, the genre saw a notable shift away from pure run-and-gun into more cerebral designs. These games thought outside the box – just what could a shooter played from first-person be?
For developer Ion Storm, the answer was a cyberpunk conspiracy thriller where progression through the story had no rules. Deus Ex begins with a choice: will you arm yourself with a tranquiliser crossbow, a sniper rifle, or a rocket launcher?
They’re more than just weapons – each option makes it clear that there are a multitude of ways to tackle the oncoming storm. Will you stealthily maneuver around the terrorists who have set up camp in New York City? Headshot them from afar? Or blow your enemies to smithereens? This guiding light asks you to consider the wider possibilities – if a door is locked, could you sneak in another way? Or can you simply blow it off its hinges? The answer to both is yes. And those solutions are arguably two of the most basic approaches on offer. Deus Ex is smart, and even 25 years later it’s easy to stumble across new possibilities on repeat playthroughs.
The series had a brief modern resurgence with two brilliant prequel games – Human Revolution and Mankind Divided – although both are arguably less complex than their parent. But even if few have rivalled its malleability, Deus Ex opened the FPS up and gave it permission to think much, much bigger.
The System Shock games of the late ‘90s whisked us away to abandoned space stations, where the story of their demise was gradually revealed through audio logs recorded by the long-dead. The series' successor, BioShock , adopted that framework while doubling down on the action. It loaded you up with not just an arsenal of guns, but also a collection of mutant abilities – including ice blasts that could freeze and fireballs that could melt – that proved the shock to the system that the FPS desperately needed in the late 2000s.
Developer Irrational Games' most striking achievement, though, was creating a post-fall world that felt truly tragic. The underwater city of Rapture will forever be one of gaming’s best locations – its sprawling corridors and chambers hauntingly drawn in art deco brass and wood, populated by insane survivors, and given life by the fascinating ecosystem of gene-harvesting Little Sisters and their Big Daddy protectors. Combined with a story that smartly challenges not just Ayn Rand’s controversial politics, but also the assumptions of the player at the controls, BioShock is one of gaming’s unforgettable triumphs.
Irrational wasn’t just making philosophical statements in the 2000s, though – it also created one of history’s greatest tactical shooters. SWAT 4 puts you in command of a team of armed officers and deploys you into a series of crime scenes across New York City, where you’ll need to deal with objectives torn from the headlines. Bomb threats, hostage situations, nightclub shootings, and even hauling in a deranged serial killer are just some of the situations you’ll need to assess and contain.
SWAT is dedicated to realism, so not only do you have to carefully order your team to scout rooms and issue orders in the correct sequence, but you also have to follow strict rules of engagement. Deaths are to be avoided at all cost, so non-lethal weapons are often your best option, and all suspects need to be arrested to achieve the optimum outcome. It all makes for an incredibly methodical shooter that rewards patience, planning, and perfect aim.
There’s not much you can really do to innovate on the FPS formula. Different kinds of guns, unique levels, or interesting mechanics only go so far to dress up the core “pull trigger to make thing die” mode of interaction, and first-person brain-burners like Portal, while ingenious, don’t quite live up to the “shooter” side of the equation. Superhot is the exception, turning the core FPS verbs of movement and shooting into an intricate, mesmerizing puzzle.
The 2016 indie sensation introduces a simple twist: time only moves when you do. Charging red enemies, rendered as stylized polygon humanoids, slow to a crawl while their bullets freeze in mid-air, letting you look around and plan your precious actions. You can shoot a pistol out of their hand, empty the magazine into your foe, fling the empty weapon at another and grab their shotgun before they can pull the trigger. SUPERHOT is a triumph of trial-and-error design made palatable by quick restarts and a huge possibility space. We haven’t seen anything like it since, save for SUPERHOT VR, which turns the clever experiment into a trippy, full-body experience that’s arguably the superior way to play.
Valve’s dedication to authentic reality has guided Half-Life through a couple of industry-leading breakthroughs. Half-Life 2’s revolutionary physics introduced the laws of gravity in a way that has never truly been matched. But Valve’s most impressive reality has been virtual – Half-Life: Alyx is so ridiculously good that it alone (almost) justifies the cost of a VR headset. Transporting you onto the streets of City 17, this is a classic narrative FPS campaign completely recalibrated for virtual reality.
Your own limbs’ physical reflexes can’t compare to the twitch controls of a mouse and keyboard, so Half-Life’s famously slippery firefights have been replaced with smaller scale battles. That may initially sound like a backstep, but the tension of being in a lethal shootout has never felt so real. Meanwhile, the zombie scares are dialed up to 11 (one of the best sequences asks you to literally cover your own mouth to mask your panicked breathing, lest an undead beast find you), and puzzles have been formatted to make full use of 3D space and tactile props. It all adds up to a world that you can really feel, and an adventure that’s more immediate than anything on a flat screen. It’s the best shooter the format has offered, but unfortunately few studios have the resources to follow in Valve’s footsteps.
FPS games began as cramped affairs, trapped in mazes scrounging for keycards or pitted against opponents in bespoke arenas. The format is well-suited for ripping and tearing through demons or teabagging noobs in Midship, but one of the biggest benefits to a first-person perspective is immersion, the idea that we’re looking into an imaginary world through someone else’s eyes. It’s a format that invites exploration, and some of the genre’s greatest games make the most of a wide-open world.
The first two Metro games are deeply atmospheric linear shooters that inject the rough shape of Half-Life with an overdose of grim Eastern European horror. They’re good, but the series’ third entry, Metro Exodus , is a genuine all-timer. Released from Moscow’s underground tunnels and sent to find your destiny on the apocalyptic surface, you’re free to approach a chain of open hub worlds in any way you wish, be that striking from the shadows or unloading both barrels into anything that moves. A mix of smart human enemies and vicious mutants ensures all combat encounters keep you on your toes, and you’ll need to master a multitude of playstyles in order to effectively survive.
If those expertly designed open environments were all Exodus had going for it, then it’d still be a fantastic FPS. But it’s elevated to masterpiece status by its story, which neatly interlocks with the game’s brutal combat mechanics to create one of the most effective horror experiences of the era.
The FPS doesn’t get much bigger than Cyberpunk 2077 . CD Projekt Red’s sci-fi masterpiece follows many of Deus Ex’s cues, including a vast array of body augmentations to unlock fascinating new playstyles, and level design that allows stealthy infiltrations, tactical hacking, and all-out gunfights. But unlike its leather-clad Y2K cousin, Cyberpunk 2077 is an epic-scale RPG set in a sprawling open world city.
The narrative demands of that massive footprint means 2077 is second to none when it comes to worldbuilding – every street corner, market arcade, and towering megablock bleeds lore and environmental storytelling. As the rough-and-ready mercenary, V, you’ll take on seedy jobs featuring some of the genre’s most compelling storylines, from edge-of-your-seat espionage infiltrations to meditations on sin. In short, it has all the top-shelf quest design you’d expect from the developers of The Witcher, but you can make your enemies explode with guns that shoot homing bullets. It’s nothing short of preem.
Ubisoft is one of the main culprits behind the modern open-world formula. Through Assassin’s Creed, the French developer popularized many of the genre’s most recognizable tropes, from climbing towers to reveal the landscape, enemy outposts scattered throughout progress-gated zones, and a minimap clogged with hundreds of icons. Far Cry 3 isn’t Ubisoft’s first attempt at an open world, but it’s the first time that the series took the lessons learned from its third-person contemporaries and applied them through a first-person lens.
Coming off of the unfriendly, unforgiving, and still-unmatched intensity of Far Cry 2, the third game is where the series entered the triple-A canon. It applies the Assassin’s Creed framework to an uncharted island, with gorgeous tropical visuals placed front and center in your field of view. The gunplay and exploration are top-notch, but what distinguishes Far Cry 3 is its story and characters. But, around the turn of the millenium, the genre saw a notable shift away from pure run-and-gun into more cerebral designs. These games thought outside the box – just what could a shooter played from first-person be?

For developer Ion Storm, the answer was a cyberpunk conspiracy thriller where progression through the story had no rules. Deus Ex begins with a choice: will you arm yourself with a tranquiliser crossbow, a sniper rifle, or a rocket launcher?

They’re more than just weapons – each option makes it clear that there are a multitude of ways to tackle the oncoming storm. Will you stealthily maneuver around the terrorists who have set up camp in New York City? Headshot them from afar? Or blow your enemies to smithereens? This guiding light asks you to consider the wider possibilities – if a door is locked, could you sneak in another way? Or can you simply blow it off its hinges? The answer to both is yes. And those solutions are arguably two of the most basic approaches on offer. Deus Ex is smart, and even 25 years later it’s easy to stumble across new possibilities on repeat playthroughs.

The series had a brief modern resurgence with two brilliant prequel games – Human Revolution and Mankind Divided – although both are arguably less complex than their parent. But even if few have rivalled its malleability, Deus Ex opened the FPS up and gave it permission to think much, much bigger.

The System Shock games of the late ‘90s whisked us away to abandoned space stations, where the story of their demise was gradually revealed through audio logs recorded by the long-dead. The series' successor, BioShock , adopted that framework while doubling down on the action. It loaded you up with not just an arsenal of guns, but also a collection of mutant abilities – including ice blasts that could freeze and fireballs that could melt – that proved the shock to the system that the FPS desperately needed in the late 2000s.

Developer Irrational Games' most striking achievement, though, was creating a post-fall world that felt truly tragic. The underwater city of Rapture will forever be one of gaming’s best locations – its sprawling corridors and chambers hauntingly drawn in art deco brass and wood, populated by insane survivors, and given life by the fascinating ecosystem of gene-harvesting Little Sisters and their Big Daddy protectors. Combined with a story that smartly challenges not just Ayn Rand’s controversial politics, but also the assumptions of the player at the controls, BioShock is one of gaming’s unforgettable triumphs.

Irrational wasn’t just making philosophical statements in the 2000s, though – it also created one of history’s greatest tactical shooters. SWAT 4 puts you in command of a team of armed officers and deploys you into a series of crime scenes across New York City, where you’ll need to deal with objectives torn from the headlines. Bomb threats, hostage situations, nightclub shootings, and even hauling in a deranged serial killer are just some of the situations you’ll need to assess and contain.

SWAT is dedicated to realism, so not only do you have to carefully order your team to scout rooms and issue orders in the correct sequence, but you also have to follow strict rules of engagement. Deaths are to be avoided at all cost, so non-lethal weapons are often your best option, and all suspects need to be arrested to achieve the optimum outcome. It all makes for an incredibly methodical shooter that rewards patience, planning, and perfect aim.

There’s not much you can really do to innovate on the FPS formula. Different kinds of guns, unique levels, or interesting mechanics only go so far to dress up the core “pull trigger to make thing die” mode of interaction, and first-person brain-burners like Portal, while ingenious, don’t quite live up to the “shooter” side of the equation. Superhot is the exception, turning the core FPS verbs of movement and shooting into an intricate, mesmerizing puzzle.

The 2016 indie sensation introduces a simple twist: time only moves when you do. Charging red enemies, rendered as stylized polygon humanoids, slow to a crawl while their bullets freeze in mid-air, letting you look around and plan your precious actions. You can shoot a pistol out of their hand, empty the magazine into your foe, fling the empty weapon at another and grab their shotgun before they can pull the trigger. SUPERHOT is a triumph of trial-and-error design made palatable by quick restarts and a huge possibility space. We haven’t seen anything like it since, save for SUPERHOT VR, which turns the clever experiment into a trippy, full-body experience that’s arguably the superior way to play.

Valve’s dedication to authentic reality has guided Half-Life through a couple of industry-leading breakthroughs. Half-Life 2’s revolutionary physics introduced the laws of gravity in a way that has never truly been matched. But Valve’s most impressive reality has been virtual – Half-Life: Alyx is so ridiculously good that it alone (almost) justifies the cost of a VR headset. Transporting you onto the streets of City 17, this is a classic narrative FPS campaign completely recalibrated for virtual reality.

Your own limbs’ physical reflexes can’t compare to the twitch controls of a mouse and keyboard, so Half-Life’s famously slippery firefights have been replaced with smaller scale battles. That may initially sound like a backstep, but the tension of being in a lethal shootout has never felt so real. Meanwhile, the zombie scares are dialed up to 11 (one of the best sequences asks you to literally cover your own mouth to mask your panicked breathing, lest an undead beast find you), and puzzles have been formatted to make full use of 3D space and tactile props. It all adds up to a world that you can really feel, and an adventure that’s more immediate than anything on a flat screen. It’s the best shooter the format has offered, but unfortunately few studios have the resources to follow in Valve’s footsteps.

FPS games began as cramped affairs, trapped in mazes scrounging for keycards or pitted against opponents in bespoke arenas. The format is well-suited for ripping and tearing through demons or teabagging noobs in Midship, but one of the biggest benefits to a first-person perspective is immersion, the idea that we’re looking into an imaginary world through someone else’s eyes. It’s a format that invites exploration, and some of the genre’s greatest games make the most of a wide-open world.

The first two Metro games are deeply atmospheric linear shooters that inject the rough shape of Half-Life with an overdose of grim Eastern European horror. They’re good, but the series’ third entry, Metro Exodus , is a genuine all-timer. Released from Moscow’s underground tunnels and sent to find your destiny on the apocalyptic surface, you’re free to approach a chain of open hub worlds in any way you wish, be that striking from the shadows or unloading both barrels into anything that moves. A mix of smart human enemies and vicious mutants ensures all combat encounters keep you on your toes, and you’ll need to master a multitude of playstyles in order to effectively survive.

If those expertly designed open environments were all Exodus had going for it, then it’d still be a fantastic FPS. But it’s elevated to masterpiece status by its story, which neatly interlocks with the game’s brutal combat mechanics to create one of the most effective horror experiences of the era.

The FPS doesn’t get much bigger than Cyberpunk 2077 . CD Projekt Red’s sci-fi masterpiece follows many of Deus Ex’s cues, including a vast array of body augmentations to unlock fascinating new playstyles, and level design that allows stealthy infiltrations, tactical hacking, and all-out gunfights. But unlike its leather-clad Y2K cousin, Cyberpunk 2077 is an epic-scale RPG set in a sprawling open world city.

The narrative demands of that massive footprint means 2077 is second to none when it comes to worldbuilding – every street corner, market arcade, and towering megablock bleeds lore and environmental storytelling. As the rough-and-ready mercenary, V, you’ll take on seedy jobs featuring some of the genre’s most compelling storylines, from edge-of-your-seat espionage infiltrations to meditations on sin. In short, it has all the top-shelf quest design you’d expect from the developers of The Witcher, but you can make your enemies explode with guns that shoot homing bullets. It’s nothing short of preem.

Ubisoft is one of the main culprits behind the modern open-world formula. Through Assassin’s Creed, the French developer popularized many of the genre’s most recognizable tropes, from climbing towers to reveal the landscape, enemy outposts scattered throughout progress-gated zones, and a minimap clogged with hundreds of icons. Far Cry 3 isn’t Ubisoft’s first attempt at an open world, but it’s the first time that the series took the lessons learned from its third-person contemporaries and applied them through a first-person lens.

Coming off of the unfriendly, unforgiving, and still-unmatched intensity of Far Cry 2, the third game is where the series entered the triple-A canon. It applies the Assassin’s Creed framework to an uncharted island, with gorgeous tropical visuals placed front and center in your field of view. The gunplay and exploration are top-notch, but what distinguishes Far Cry 3 is its story and characters.
